  2. 2. Major Scales and Key Signatures

Major Scales and Key Signatures: From Do to the Names

Chapter 2 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom for students who already read and write in major with movable do: half and whole steps, scale degrees, and key signatures as new names for what they already audiate.

This page goes with Chapter 2, Major Scales and Key Signatures of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom.

You already know this. You can sing in major tonality on movable do, find do on the staff, and read and write tonal patterns. This chapter adds no new sounds. It gives names to things you already hear and write. Each section below starts from what you know, then gives the textbook’s word for it.

Press ▶ to hear an example, or ▶ Sing to hear it sung on syllables. Click any heading to fold its section.

What you know → what the book calls it

You say (MLT) The book says (Hutchinson ch. 2)
major tonality major key, major scale
do, the resting tone tonic, scale degree 1 (written 1̂)
do re mi fa so la ti scale degrees 1̂ 2̂ 3̂ 4̂ 5̂ 6̂ 7̂
the close steps mi–fa and ti–do half steps
every other step (do–re, re–mi …) whole steps
keyality (where you sing do, e.g. G) the key’s name: “G major”
the do signature the key signature

2.1 Half steps and whole steps

Sing the major scale up on syllables and listen to the size of each step. Two of them are smaller: mi–fa and ti–do. The book calls a small step a half step (on a keyboard, the very next key) and a big one a whole step (two half steps). Read 2.1

So the pattern of steps in every major scale is W W H W W W H. That isn’t a new rule to learn: it’s the shape of the scale you already sing, written down.

On the staff. In C, the half steps fall on E–F and B–C, where there is no black key between. That’s why C major needs no sharps or flats. Start the same pattern on another note and some letters have to change to keep the half steps on mi–fa and ti–do. That is all a key signature is.

2.2 Scale degrees and their names

The book numbers the notes of the scale from do: 1̂ to 7̂. Each also has a name. Read 2.2

Syllable Degree Name
do 1̂ tonic
re 2̂ supertonic
mi 3̂ mediant
fa 4̂ subdominant
so 5̂ dominant
la 6̂ submediant
ti 7̂ leading tone

(The degree names are standard; Hutchinson’s own list is in 3.3 Scale Degree Names.)

You already sing tonic and dominant patterns: do–mi–so is a tonic pattern, so–ti–re a dominant pattern. Those words come from these degree names: the patterns are built on do (the tonic) and so (the dominant).

Do and the tonic. Usually the same note in major, but not always the same idea. Do is a syllable and moves with the keyality. Tonic is the resting tone of whatever key you are in. In minor you rest on la, and the book will call la the tonic of the minor key (Chapter 3).

2.3 Key signatures are do signatures

You already find do from the key signature. Gordon calls a key signature a do signature: it shows where do is on the staff, and nothing more. The same signature can be major, minor, Dorian and so on, depending on which note the music rests on (Gordon 155–156). Read 2.3

The book reads a signature as the name of a major key, which is the same as asking “where is do?”:

  • Sharps: the last sharp is ti. Do is the next note up. Last sharp F♯ → do is G → G major.
  • Flats: the last flat is fa. Do is four notes down (or five up). With two or more flats, the second-to-last flat is do: B♭ E♭ → do is B♭ → B♭ major. One flat (B♭) → do is F.

Here is the same tune with three different do signatures. Your syllables stay the same, only the letters change:

Where the book and MLT disagree. Hutchinson reads three flats as “E♭ major or C minor”. Gordon reads it as do on E♭, and the music decides the rest: E♭ major if it rests on do, C minor if it rests on la, F Dorian if on re (Gordon 155–156). Both are right; the book names the two keys you’ll meet most often.

Practise: name the major key

Name the major key from the signature (that is, find do). Start with up to three sharps and flats in treble clef, then open Settings and add more.

Bridging: from syllables to letters

The book expects you to write scales and key signatures from letter names. You can already write tonal patterns from a familiar do signature (Gordon 125). To get from there to the book’s tasks:

  1. Name do. Look at the signature and say the letter of do aloud (“do is D”).
  2. Sing, then spell. Sing do re mi fa so la ti do, and say each letter as you go: D E F♯ G A B C♯ D. If a letter sounds wrong for the syllable, it needs an accidental.
  3. Check the half steps. mi–fa and ti–do should be the only neighbours with no key between them.
  4. Go the other way. Given “write A♭ major”, put do on A♭, sing up, and write each letter. Then collect the accidentals: that’s the key signature.

Check yourself

  1. In D major, which letters are mi and fa?
  2. Name the major key with four sharps.
  3. Name the major key with four flats.
  4. Which scale degree is so? What is its name?
  5. Write the steps (W or H) between each note of A major.
TipAnswers
  1. F♯ and G.
  2. E major (last sharp D♯ is ti).
  3. A♭ major (second-to-last flat).
  4. 5̂, the dominant.
  5. W W H W W W H, the same as every major scale: A B C♯ D E F♯ G♯ A.

All the key-signature drills are on Theory Drills. Next: Meter: Two Ways to Sort Time Signatures and Rhythm Notation from Du De. Related: Modes: Three Meanings of One Word.
